articles.title: How to Consume a Job from a Message Queue in Node.js (Weekly Digest)
articles.excerpt: To consume a job from a message queue in Node.js, send it through the queue's consume API, run an idempotent worker, then acknowledge the message only after the weekly digest result is durable. Use a…
articles.body: To consume a job from a message queue in Node.js, send it through the queue's consume API, run an idempotent worker, then acknowledge the message only after the weekly digest result is durable. Use a workflow engine when the digest is a multi-step process with durable state, joins, or long-running orchestration. That is the decision rule. For a fintech product, the important invariant is not “the worker ran once.” It is “each customer’s digest has one durable business result, even if delivery happens more than once.” Standard queues are at-least-once, so idempotency belongs in the consumer. A successful message should be acknowledged and removed; a failed one should be retried or moved toward a dead-letter queue instead of disappearing.

articles.body: The situation repeats itself: I walk into a company as its fractional CTO, the engineering org is a few dozen developers, and nobody — not the CEO, not the VP R&D, not the team leads — can answer "what is everyone working on?" without opening four different trackers. The first week decides whether you're credible or just another consultant. Here's what I actually do with those seven days. What I stopped doing I stopped asking for status reports. I stopped asking for slide decks. Both are already out of date by the time they reach you, and both are written by the people you're supposed to be checking on. Nobody in an 80-developer department is lying to you. Everyone is just reading a different tracker, and none of them match. What I look at instead, in order 1.

articles.title: Browser Storage Upload: Webhook Notification Rules for Private-Bucket Retention, Thumbnails, and Virus-Scan Processing
articles.excerpt: Short answer: let the browser upload a signed object into a private quarantine bucket, then let a verified storage event create the scan and thumbnail job; the application, not the browser, should enf…
articles.body: Short answer: let the browser upload a signed object into a private quarantine bucket, then let a verified storage event create the scan and thumbnail job; the application, not the browser, should enforce the deletion deadline. That decision fits a customer-support system retaining signed documents. It also draws a line that is easy to miss: an upload being durable does not mean the file is safe to show, and a successful scan does not mean the file may be retained forever. I would record the deadline beside the document before issuing the upload authorization, then make every later state transition carry that deadline. What must the retention-first upload architecture guarantee? The first invariant is private ingress.

articles.title: Storing Generated Images — Object Storage Is Better Than Relational Databases Explained
articles.excerpt: TL;DR: Put the generated image bytes in object storage and keep a small, transactional record in the relational database. The database should answer who owns an image, which prompt produced it, and wh…
articles.body: TL;DR: Put the generated image bytes in object storage and keep a small, transactional record in the relational database. The database should answer who owns an image, which prompt produced it, and whether the audit copy is complete. It should not carry the growing byte stream through every transaction, backup, replica, and query path. That division matters even more in a developer-tools system that processes receipts. A receipt may be an ordinary image, a generated reconstruction, or a transformed derivative, but the original file still has to survive for audit. Large-file throughput is the constraint that changes the design: the application should stream bytes to a durable object key, then commit metadata that points to that key. The better boundary is usually the boring one.

articles.title: My screenshot was 1080x1350. The page was 1722 pixels tall.
articles.excerpt: A piece of artwork went live last month without the contact line at the bottom. Phone, handle and site were in the HTML, the CSS placed them, the browser laid them out, and the file that got published…
articles.body: A piece of artwork went live last month without the contact line at the bottom. Phone, handle and site were in the HTML, the CSS placed them, the browser laid them out, and the file that got published did not contain them. Three checks ran before publishing, and all three passed. What the check asked The pipeline was short: render a local HTML file, screenshot it, verify it. Verification asked two questions. Is the image 1080 by 1350? It is. Does each element sit inside its own box, with no overlap and no text against the edge? Yes. Nobody asked whether the file contained the whole page. The image had the dimensions from the request, and the layout assertions had run against a live DOM whose document was 1722 pixels tall.

articles.title: Why did my AWS bill go up? How to find the cause in 10 minutes
articles.excerpt: Your bill is higher than last month and nothing obvious changed. Traffic is flat, nobody launched anything big, and the invoice is one long list of line items. The good news: AWS records exactly where…
articles.body: Your bill is higher than last month and nothing obvious changed. Traffic is flat, nobody launched anything big, and the invoice is one long list of line items. The good news: AWS records exactly where every cent went. Finding the cause is a matter of narrowing it down in the right order — service, then usage type, then region . Step 1: compare like with like The most common mistake is comparing this month so far with the whole of last month. Ten days of spending will always look smaller than thirty, and a real spike hides behind it. Compare the same days of each month instead: the 1st to the 10th of this month against the 1st to the 10th of last month. Step 2: find the service that moved In the console: Billing and Cost Management → Cost Explorer .
